{{Short description|Italian physicist (1931–2026)}}
'''Daniele Amati''' (11 August 1931 – 4 August 2026) was an Italian theoretical physicist, specialising in [[particle physics]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Daniele Amati|website=SISSA|url=http://www.sissa.it/tpp/members.php?ID=12}}</ref>

==Life and career==
Amati was born in [[Rome]] on 11 August 1931.<ref>{{cite web|author=Dell'Arti, Giorgio|title=Biografia di Daniele Amati|year=2015|website=cinquantamila.it|url=http://www.cinquantamila.it/storyTellerThread.php?threadId=AMATI%20Daniele}}</ref> In 1952 he received, from the [[University of Buenos Aires]], his Ph.D. in physics under [[Richard Gans]] with a thesis on ferroresonant circuits. In 1953–1954 Amati was a fellow at the [[Centro Brasileiro de Pesquisas Físicas]] in California, where he took several graduate courses, including one taught by [[Richard Feynman]].<ref>{{cite arXiv|author=Sirlin, Alberto|authorlink=Alberto Sirlin|title=Remembering a Great Teacher|year=2015|eprint=1512.08247|class=physics.hist-ph}}</ref> From 1954 to 1959 Amati was an assistant at the University of Rome. Afterwards he was in the theory department of [[CERN]] and from 1973 to 1975 its director. Since 1986 he has been a professor at and, until 2001, director of the [[Scuola Internazionale Superiore di Studi Avanzati]] (SISSA). SISSA not only deals with physics but also with cognitive science and biology and is close to the [[International Center for Theoretical Physics]] (ICTP) located near Trieste. Under the auspices of SISSA, [[Springer Nature]] publishes the purely electronic ''[[Journal of High Energy Physics]]'', founded by Amati in 1997. In the early to mid-1970s, Amati made the theory group at CERN a center of early [[string theory]] development, which was initiated as a result of a dual-resonance model by [[Gabriele Veneziano]] at CERN in 1968.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Alessandrini, Victor|author2=Amati, D.|author3=Le Bellac, Michel|author4=Olive, D.|authorlink4=David Olive|title=The Operator Approach to Dual Multiparticle Theory|journal=Physics Reports |volume=1|issue=6|year=1971|pages=269–345|doi=10.1016/0370-1573(71)90008-1|bibcode=1971PhR.....1..269A}}</ref> Among CERN's theory group, Victor Alessandrini in 1971 and [[Claud Lovelace]] in 1970 published on the multiloop amplitudes of the bosonic string.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Alessandrini, V.|title=A general approach to dual multiloop diagrams|journal=Il Nuovo Cimento|date=March 1971|volume=2|issue=2|pages=321–352|doi=10.1007/BF02899858|url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/351483|bibcode=1971NCimA...2..321A|s2cid=124534333|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Lovelace, C.|title=M-loop generalized Veneziano formula|volume=32|issue=8|journal=Phys. Lett. B|date=14 September 1970|pages=703–708|doi=10.1016/0370-2693(70)90450-8|url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/350799|bibcode=1970PhLB...32..703L}}</ref><ref>{{citation|chapter=Dual amplitudes in higher dimensions: a personal view|last=Lovelace|first=Claud|pages=198–201|title=The Birth of String Theory|editor-last=Cappelli|editor-first=Andrea|editor-last2=Castellani|editor-first2=Elena|editor-last3=Colomo|editor-first3=Filipo|editor-last4=Di Vecchia|editor-first4=Paolo| display-editors = 3|year=2012|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|isbn=978-0-521-19790-8|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WNZyoUteXIkC&pg=PA198}}.</ref> Amati's 1989 article with Ciafaloni and Veneziano has over 1000 citations.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Amati, D.|author2=Ciafaloni, M.|author3=Veneziano, G.|title=Can spacetime be probed below the string size?|journal=Physics Letters B|volume=216|issue=1–2|date=5 January 1989|pages=41–47|doi=10.1016/0370-2693(89)91366-X|url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/191788|bibcode=1989PhLB..216...41A}}</ref>

{{blockquote|Back in the early 1970s, Italian physicist Daniele Amati, characterized string theory as "part of 21st-century physics that fell by chance into the 20th-century." He meant that string theory had been invented by a process of tinkering, without physicists really grasping what was behind it. Amati surmised that a true understanding of the foundations of this remarkably rich theory would have to await the 21st century.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Witten, Edward|authorlink=Edward Witten|title=Universe on a String|journal=Astronomy|volume=30|pages=45 of 44–47|url=http://www.sns.ias.edu/ckfinder/userfiles/files/string(3).pdf|archive-date=2015-07-14|access-date=2018-06-30|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150714120831/http://www.sns.ias.edu/ckfinder/userfiles/files/string(3).pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>}}

Amati died in [[Trieste]] on 4 August 2026, at the age of 94.<ref>[https://www.ilpiccolo.it/cronaca/daniele-amati-morto-scienza-fisica-sissa-trieste-cern-ju3yknmj Il mondo scientifico piange Daniele Amati: fisico di fama mondiale, fu direttore della Sissa di Trieste] {{in lang|it}}</ref>
